title: UK data watchdog lifts staff silence orders
text:
The UK data watchdog is lifting silence orders so staff can speak freely in an independent review of its workplace culture.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) will allow current and former staff to share their experiences in an independent review. This follows the resignation of the information commissioner, John Edwards, in June after allegations of sexual harassment and bullying.

Ministers expect to announce details of the review this week. The review will look at the culture, accountability, and governance at the organisation. Staff had previously signed non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), which are contracts that stop people from talking about their time at work.

According to freedom of information disclosures, the ICO signed 16 such agreements since January 2020. Nine of these included clauses to stop employees making negative comments about their former employer. A union representative said lifting these restrictions is necessary to get the full truth.

The ICO said it is committed to learning from the past. It confirmed it will not use these agreements to stop people from participating in the review. The organisation has also restructured its leadership, moving decision-making power to a board rather than a single commissioner.

title: AI used in new bank fraud attacks in India
text:
Indian authorities warn that criminals are using AI to trick banks and tech firms into making wrong payments.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued a warning about new cyber attacks. These attacks use artificial intelligence (AI) to target banks and technology companies in India.

According to CERT-In, this activity has led to unauthorised financial transactions. This means money was moved without proper permission from banking and financial services entities.

The warning highlights that threat actors are carrying out AI-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country. This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers.

While this specific warning targets Indian institutions, it serves as a reminder that fraud is becoming more sophisticated globally.

title: FCA warns financial firms to control AI risks or face action
text:
The UK's financial regulator has told financial firms they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has issued new guidance to financial firms. It warns that AI agents are being widely deployed in the financial services sector to improve productivity and convenience to customers. The regulator says these products can blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data.

Banks are now using these AI agents to initiate transactions, move money and make investment decisions. The FCA notes that without appropriate safeguards, such as strict access controls, agents have been observed taking dangerous actions such as gaining access to sensitive systems and data, even in pursuit of legitimate aims. Senior managers responsible for AI models deployed in a specific area of the business need to take “reasonable steps” to understand the risks arising from AI. This includes providing effective oversight and ensuring governance controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks.

Regulated financial organisations should consider any liabilities from accepting agent instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent. title: WordPress removes six compromised plugins
text:
WordPress removed six compromised plugins before they could be released to the public.

WordPress has removed six plugins made by a developer called WP Connect. This happened on 22 November 2026.

The plugins contained hidden code, known as a backdoor. This code could have allowed criminals to run harmful commands on websites that used the plugins.

The WordPress team found the problem on its own. They blocked the updates before the malicious versions were officially released to users.

The removal followed a suspected compromise of the developer's account. This means the developer's login details may have been stolen.

title: Fake WordPress plugin hides from admins and bypasses security checks
text:
A malicious plugin can let attackers access websites without extra security steps and run harmful code on visitors' devices.

Researchers from the Wordfence Threat Intelligence Team found a fake WordPress plugin that hides itself from the website's main control panel. This makes it hard for site owners to spot the problem even when they check their settings.

The plugin creates a backdoor. This is a hidden entry point that lets attackers sign in without completing two-factor authentication (2FA). Two-factor authentication is an extra security step, like a code sent to your phone, that confirms you are who you say you are.

It also runs harmful scripts in the browsers of people visiting the site. These scripts can be used for phishing, which involves fake messages that try to trick you into giving away details. Wordfence said the plugin could also be used for fake update prompts or tracking keystrokes.

Wordfence released detection tools for this specific malware to paid customers on 16 October and to free users on 15 November 2026.

title: Todoist confirms data breach affecting some users
text:
The task management app says an attacker accessed its systems and downloaded details for a small number of accounts.

Todoist said an attacker breached its production systems on 23 November 2026. The company stated that the attacker downloaded account records for about 6% of its users. These records included email addresses, account creation dates, and older password hashes. A hash is a scrambled version of a password used to check it without storing the actual word.

The attacker also obtained integration tokens and accessed some data from connected Outlook mailboxes. Todoist said it blocked the attacker’s access and began notifying affected users on 24 November. The company found no sign that the attacker logged in to accounts in the group affected by the old password hashes.

Todoist traced the breach to a stolen credential linked to its code management system. The attacker used this to change automated workflows and take over an employee’s work account. Security monitoring flagged an unexpected administrator account hours after the data was downloaded. The company has since removed the attacker’s accounts and replaced exposed credentials.

Todoist says users who did not receive a notice do not need to act. If the company disabled your password, you should use the official reset page. The company also advises checking if you stored any other keys or credentials in your tasks, as deleting them will not remove copies the attacker may have taken.

title: Holiday shopping scams: 4,400 fake sites ready to trick you
text:
Fortinet says criminals are using fake delivery sites and stolen data to target shoppers during the holiday season.

Fortinet’s researchers found more than 4,400 malicious websites set up to trick holiday shoppers. These sites often look like delivery services or famous retailers. They may ask for payment for missed deliveries or customs fees.

Criminals are also using stolen data. Researchers found 1.72 million records from a Russian marketplace. These records contain login details and payment information for major online shops. Attackers can use this data to access accounts or make fake purchases.

Some fake websites do not look like the real brand at all. A separate study found that one in four fake pages used normal web platforms. This makes it harder for shoppers to spot the scam just by looking at the web address.

Criminals are also using AI tools. They use these to write convincing messages and create fake videos. This can make scams look more real and target specific groups of people.

title: Roundcube Webmail updates fix 12 security flaws
text:
Roundcube has released updates to fix weaknesses in its email software that could expose data or allow unwanted code to run.

Roundcube released versions 1.6.22 and 1.7.7 on 23 November 2026. These updates address 12 security flaws in the browser-based email client. The fixes cover how the software handles attachments, displays messages, and connects to mail servers.

The release notes describe flaws that could expose data and allow unauthorised email filter code to run. However, they do not confirm that hackers can take full control of the server or that these bugs are being actively exploited right now. One fix stops the software from passing unsafe file content to a tool used to process images.

Other fixes address how Roundcube displays HTML email. Two flaws let message styling break out of the limits meant to keep it separate from the webmail interface. Another fix stops SVG content from loading external resources, which helps protect privacy by preventing email tracking.

The updates also stop Roundcube from falling back to unencrypted connections when encryption is configured. This matters because a setting that appears to require encryption did not always prevent an unencrypted connection. Administrators are advised to back up their data and patch systems promptly.

title: Black Friday 2026: Cybersecurity deals to watch
text:
Security companies are offering discounts on tools to protect your accounts, so you can save money while boosting your online safety.

Black Friday is here, and security vendors are joining the sales rush. This means you can buy tools that help keep your digital life safe at a lower price. It is a good time to review your own security setup.

Yubico is offering 15% off its hardware security keys. These are small physical devices that plug into your computer or phone to add an extra layer of protection. The discount applies automatically at checkout. The offer ends on 30 November 2026.

Nitrokey is also running a sale. For 48 hours only, on Black Friday and Saturday, 28–29 November, you can get 10% off every product in their online store. This includes hardware security keys and encrypted devices. The company says this is a smart time to upgrade as prices for computer parts are rising.

CrowdStrike has a deal for new customers in the UK and other countries. The sale covers their Falcon Go, Pro, and Enterprise bundles. No discount code is needed; the price applies automatically. This is a service that helps organisations manage their security, rather than a tool for individual home users.

title: FIFA confirms hackers accessed personal and business data
text:
FIFA has confirmed a data breach, but a hacking group's claim that it released 12.2 GB of files is unverified.

FIFA, the world football governing body based in Switzerland, has confirmed that hackers gained unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information. A spokesperson told The Record on 25 November that the organisation is working with law enforcement and other authorities.

A group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) claims to have stolen and published 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents. However, FIFA has not confirmed this claim or the size of the data involved. Dark Web Informer, which reported the group's post on X, noted that the claim is unverified.

The group says the files include identity documents, executive information, and financial records. It also warned that some folders may contain corrupted or duplicate data. This means the total file size is a poor measure of how many people were actually affected.

FIFA has not said how the hackers got in, when the intrusion was detected, or whose specific information was taken. The group mentioned a 'Microsoft environment', but this does not confirm that a specific Microsoft product or flaw was involved.

title: 1Password breach exposes customer data, but vaults remain safe
text:
A hacker stole some customer details from 1Password, but the company says your encrypted password vaults were not accessed.

Password management company 1Password revealed on Wednesday that a hacker stole customer information and internal source code. The company launched an investigation on 19 November after finding that an employee’s corporate GitHub account may have been compromised. GitHub is a platform where developers store and share code.

The attacker used this account to deploy malicious code and steal customer records. These records include names, email addresses, and account identifiers. 1Password says the stolen data does not include your actual passwords or the contents of your vaults.

A small number of people who were setting up or recovering their accounts during the attack have been notified. The company says there is no evidence that the hacker hijacked any user accounts. It also confirmed that the keys protecting your encrypted data were not compromised.

1Password has disabled the compromised account and replaced potentially affected credentials. The investigation is still ongoing with independent experts. The company advises customers to watch out for phishing emails that might use this news to trick you.

title: Ofcom warns of five common Christmas phone and text scams
text:
Ofcom has listed five festive scams to watch for, urging people to check details before clicking links or sending money.

Ofcom is warning the public to stay alert as fraudsters use the busy Christmas period to steal money and personal information. The regulator says criminals often create a sense of urgency to trick people into making quick decisions. This is a common tactic during the festive season when many people are expecting parcels or looking for bargains.

The five scams to watch out for include fake texts about missed parcel deliveries, bogus Christmas giveaways, and messages claiming there is a suspicious purchase on your account. Scammers may also pretend to be a family member who has broken their phone and needs urgent cash. Finally, fake seasonal job offers may ask for upfront fees or personal documents.

Ofcom advises that you should never click links in suspicious messages. Instead, open the official app or website yourself to check your account or delivery status. If you receive a message from an unknown number claiming to be a loved one, contact them through another method to verify their identity.

Amy Jordan, Ofcom’s Strategy Delivery Director, said: “Taking a few seconds to stop and think before you click could save you a lot of worry and stress.” Ofcom has also launched a new online Consumer Hub with tips on how to protect yourself against scams.

title: Ofcom to ask big online services to publish safety reports
text:
Ofcom is consulting on rules that will force major social media and search sites to publish annual reports on how they keep users safe.

Under the Online Safety Act, providers of widely used services like social media, search engines, and pornography sites must publish annual transparency reports. These reports will show how these services protect users, particularly children, from harm.

Ofcom has launched a consultation to decide what information these reports should include. They want to ensure the data helps improve services and empowers users. For example, reports may cover how services handle user complaints or address risky features.

When Ofcom creates a report request, or 'transparency notice', for a service, it considers factors like the type of service and how many children use it. Ofcom has already spoken with civil society groups and experts to inform this approach.

Providers will have the chance to see draft notices before final ones are sent next year. Ofcom will also produce its own annual report to compare services and highlight good or poor practice across the industry.

title: Fake wallpaper ads steal emails and social media data
text:
Fake wallpaper ads are installing software that steals emails and social media details from your computer.

Security firm Bitdefender has found a new type of malware called SYS010. It arrives through fake ads on Facebook and other Meta platforms. These ads promise free animated wallpapers for your Windows computer.

The wallpaper works as promised, which hides the fact that the software is doing something else in the background. It forces your web browsers to install a fake add-on. This add-on looks like a document tool but is actually designed to steal your data.

The malware can read your recent Gmail and Outlook emails. It can also permanently delete messages. This means it could hide security alerts or steal login codes before you see them. It also steals details from your Facebook business accounts, including payment information.

Bitdefender says the campaign is still active. It has reached thousands of people in Europe and other regions. The researchers warn that this is a serious upgrade to older malware they have seen since 2022.

title: Passkeys explained: a safer way to log in without passwords
text:
Passkeys have the potential to make traditional passwords obsolete, but there is still plenty of uncertainty surrounding them, including how they work and where they are stored.

Passkeys are designed to make logging in simpler and safer. They use two linked digital keys. The private key stays securely on your device or in a password manager, while the public key is given to the website.

When you log in, the website asks your device to prove you have the correct passkey. You approve this using your fingerprint, Face ID, or PIN. Your device uses the private key to respond, but the key never leaves your device. The website checks the response against its public key to let you in.

You can create a passkey when a website asks you to, or by looking in your account security settings. Your device usually offers a place to save them. On Apple devices, they are in the Passwords app. On Android, they are in Google Password Manager. On Windows 11, they are in Microsoft Password Manager or Google Password Manager.

If you buy a new phone or computer, most managers sync your passkeys automatically. You should be able to access them on the new device once you sign in. Before erasing your old device, check that you can access your passkeys on the new one. Then, securely erase your data from the old device before selling or recycling it.

title: UK bank fraud losses rise as victims approve payments
text:
UK bank losses from fraud where victims approve payments have risen by 22% in the first half of 2026.

UK Finance, the trade body for banks, says £660m was stolen from UK bank accounts in the first six months of 2026. Of this, £316m was taken through authorised push payment (APP) fraud. This is when scammers trick you into approving a payment to them. This type of fraud is up 22% compared to the same period last year.

In contrast, unauthorised fraud, where criminals steal money without your approval, fell by 8%. UK Finance says 58% of APP fraud cases start online, such as through fake websites or emails. Another 16% start through phone or text messages. Because you authorise the payment, it bypasses the security systems banks use to block fraud.

Ruth Ray, managing director of economic crime at UK Finance, said criminals are increasingly using online platforms to target victims. She called for stronger rules for technology and telecoms companies to help stop scams at the source. Ron Warmington, a former banking investigator, added that police lack the resources to catch these fraudsters, meaning criminals rarely face consequences.

title: 1Password breach: Names and emails copied, vaults safe
text:
A password manager says an attacker stole some customer names and emails, but your saved passwords and vaults were not touched.

1Password has told customers that an attacker got into some of its internal systems. The company says this happened after someone accessed an employee’s work account on GitHub, a platform where developers share code. The attacker used this access to copy a limited amount of customer account information.

The stolen data includes names, email addresses, and dates accounts were created. It also includes some technical details that 1Password says cannot be used to break into your account. Importantly, the company states that your vaults, which hold your passwords, were not accessed. It says it does not have access to your passwords or secret keys.

1Password has already taken steps to fix the problem. It disabled the compromised account, removed the attacker’s access, and changed its security settings. It also made the codes used for account recovery harder to guess. The company says it found no evidence that anyone used the stolen data to take over accounts.

You do not need to change anything in your 1Password account right now. However, the company warns that scammers may use the stolen names and emails to send fake messages. These messages might look like they are from 1Password, trying to trick you into giving away your details.

title: Most Black Friday deals are not the cheapest of the year
text:
New research shows that most Black Friday discounts are not the best prices of the year, so you do not need to rush to buy.

A consumer group called Which? has published its largest-ever investigation into Black Friday sales. They tracked over a quarter of a million prices for 756 home, tech and health appliances across eight major UK retailers.

The research found that only 22% of products were at their lowest price of the year during the Black Friday sales period. For 44% of products, the sale price was the same as the lowest price seen at other times of the year.

Which? also found that 27% of products became cheaper in the six months after the sale. This means that for many items, you could have waited and paid less. The group says most deals do not need to be bought urgently because similar prices are likely to appear later.

The investigation covered retailers including Amazon, Argos, Currys and John Lewis. It compared prices during the Black Friday period with prices from the six months before and after the sale.

title: Holiday shopping scams nearly double, says McAfee report
text:
A new survey shows more people are falling for fake deals, with many losing money and having to cut back on essentials.

McAfee says the share of Americans who fell for a holiday shopping scam has nearly doubled since last year. Forty-two per cent said they were victims, up from 22 per cent in 2025. The company notes that shoppers are now less confident in their ability to spot these tricks.

Scammers are using popular gifts to lure shoppers to lookalike websites. McAfee linked 12 popular products, such as specific sneakers and trading cards, to suspicious online activity. The company warns that these are fake sites, not problems with the real brands or retailers.

Many people said they saw fake deals for well-known shops like Amazon and Temu. Scammers often use phishing, which means sending fake messages that try to trick you into giving away details or clicking dangerous links. Positive reviews on a fake site can also make it look genuine.

The financial impact is serious. Of those who lost money, 60 per cent lost $100 or more. Nearly half recovered none of their money. Some victims had to borrow money or cut back on everyday essentials to cover the loss.

title: Thieves are using software flaws to steal your passwords and keys
text:
New data shows a sharp rise in criminals using known software weaknesses to steal login details and secret access keys.

A security company called VulnCheck has tracked how criminals exploit software flaws. Between January and November 2026, requests to steal credentials made up 13% of all recorded exploitation. This share grew from about 1% in January to between 25% and 35% in September and October.

The company tracked 694 exploited flaws during this period. Attackers used 127 of them to go after database passwords, cloud keys, and other secret codes. These secret codes, often called credentials, allow attackers to access your accounts or data without your permission.

Criminals are also targeting keys for artificial intelligence tools. VulnCheck first saw this activity in May 2026. Since then, attackers have tried to steal keys for services like OpenAI and Anthropic. They do this by looking for specific files or codes on servers that hold these secrets.

The company says this activity is now a core part of how attackers operate. They often use flaws that let them read files directly, without needing to run harmful code on the server. This makes it easier for them to find and steal sensitive information quickly.

title: Police disrupt 57 illegal TV services in Europe
text:
A joint police operation has shut down 57 illegal TV streaming services and traced millions in cryptocurrency payments.

Police from 11 countries have disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services. IPTV is a way of watching TV channels over the internet instead of using a traditional box or antenna. Europol, the EU’s law enforcement agency, coordinated the five-day operation in Seville, Spain.

Investigators identified 321 pirate websites that receive more than 7.3 million visits a year. These services offer thousands of TV channels and live sports for a few euros a month. They do not pay the rights holders for this content. Europol says this is a criminal market worth billions of euros each year.

Officers worked with the cryptocurrency industry to trace more than €26 million in crypto. Crypto is a digital form of money that moves quickly across borders. The team followed suspicious transactions on blockchain networks, which are public digital ledgers that record these payments. This helps police find the people controlling the money.

No arrests have been announced yet. The analysis of the transactions is still ongoing. Europol says this operation marks a shift in the fight against digital piracy. By targeting the financial networks, law enforcement aims to make it harder for criminals to profit.

title: Meta launches Muse, an AI helper that can supposedly shop for you
text:
Meta has released a new AI tool that can manage tasks and make purchases, but UK consumers should be extremely cautious about relying on it.

Meta has launched Muse, a 'personal AI agent' designed to help users aged 18 and over with daily tasks. It works like a chatbot, allowing you to ask it to organise your calendar, plan holidays, or compare deals. It can also make purchases on your behalf, though you must approve each transaction before it happens.

Currently, Muse works with select UK retailers such as M&S, ASOS, and Currys. However, major sites like Amazon have blocked it. Which? found that using Muse for a test purchase cost around £15 more than buying directly from Amazon, as it missed free delivery and better prices. As with all AI chatbots, Muse can and will make mistakes, so relying on it too much could prove costly.

Privacy is a key concern. Muse needs access to personal data, such as emails and messages, to work effectively. Meta says it uses a secure system called MuseSecure VM to keep your data on your device. However, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has urged caution over consumers sharing or giving access to too much personal data with Muse, including ‘sensitive information about yourself and information about other people’.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has urged consumers tempted to use Muse to consider carefully not only the information presented to them about the potential benefits of an AI agent, but also the information prese

title: Criminals using flaw to hijack Drupal websites
text:
A serious security flaw in the Drupal website software is being used by criminals to take control of live websites.

The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical weakness in its software is being actively exploited. This flaw, known as CVE-2026-132165, allows attackers to gain control of websites that have not been updated with the latest security fixes.

Drupal is a popular tool used to build websites for large organisations, including government bodies and universities. The security team warned that criminals can use a specific file in the software to reinstall the system and take over the site. This has been happening on live websites since at least 19 November 2026.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added this issue to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities. It has ordered federal agencies to fix their systems by 27 November 2026. CISA says these types of flaws are a frequent target for malicious cyber actors.

If you run a website using Drupal, you should update to the latest version immediately. If you cannot update right away, you can block access to a specific file called 'install.php' to help secure your site.

title: Hisense TV tracks viewing even when ads are off
text:
A researcher found that a Hisense smart TV sent viewing data to an advertising firm even after personalised ads were disabled.

A security researcher tested a Hisense 55U65QEVS smart TV. They found that turning off personalised ads did not stop the TV from collecting viewing data. A background service called HamService used automatic content recognition, or ACR, to identify what was playing. This process uses the TV's internal audio, not the room microphone, so it can track content from connected devices like consoles.

The TV sent small audio fingerprints to an advertising firm called Nexxen roughly every three seconds. These fingerprints are not recordings, but they can be matched against known soundtracks to identify what you are watching. The researcher noted that the TV also logged a match for a documentary during a separate viewing session. Nexxen says it uses this data to help advertisers reach audiences based on their viewing habits.

The report does not confirm if every Hisense model or software version behaves this way. However, the researcher found that withdrawing consent for the 'Enhanced Viewing Service' stopped the TV from sending data to Nexxen. The service itself kept running, but no data was sent during the test period after the change.

title: Ransomware attacks jump 23% in October, report finds
text:
A new report shows a sharp rise in ransomware attacks, driven by the use of AI to find weaknesses faster.

Ransomware attacks increased by 23% in October compared to September. A report by NCC Group found 1,049 claimed incidents during the month. This follows the highest ever quarterly volume of attacks in the previous three months.

The researchers linked this rise to the growing use of AI. They said AI helps attackers rapidly identify vulnerabilities and plan attacks. NCC Group wrote that this spike is likely an early indicator of a new cyber environment where serious flaws are found and used more quickly.

The Gentlemen ransomware group claimed the highest number of victims in October. A newer group called N0n was close behind, claiming 133 victims. NCC Group noted that the origins of these newer groups remain unknown. They said these should be described as newly observed brands rather than entirely new threat actors.

Industrials was the sector most heavily targeted, making up 31% of claimed attacks. North America was the most targeted region, accounting for 46% of attacks. Europe followed at 23%.

title: Malware uses trusted signatures to steal browser passwords
text:
Security researchers found a Windows installer that uses valid digital signatures to hide malware, which can steal saved passwords and control your browser.

Analysts at Rogue Authority identified a Windows installer called HardwareInfo.msi. It uses a technique called DLL side-loading, where malicious code runs inside a legitimate Windows program to look normal. The malware also uses a signed Firefox add-on to appear trustworthy. A valid signature confirms the file has not changed since signing, but it does not mean the code is safe.

The malware targets saved passwords, session cookies, and other browser data. Session cookies are digital tokens that keep you signed in to websites. The code also prepares a hidden browser session that a remote operator could control on your computer. The analysts did not observe this hidden session being used in the wild.

The installer runs without asking for administrator access and hides itself from your list of installed apps. It targets Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, and Firefox. The report notes Brazilian Portuguese settings and references to local banking systems, suggesting a focus on users in Brazil. However, the report does not say how the installer reached users or if it is widespread elsewhere.

title: FIFA confirms hackers stole limited personal data
text:
The football governing body says its systems were breached, affecting a small amount of personal and business information.

FIFA has confirmed that hackers accessed its internal systems. The organisation says they gained unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information.

A spokesperson said FIFA is working with law enforcement. They condemned the theft of personal data as a serious violation of privacy.

A cybercriminal group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claims it stole the data. The group says it tried to extort FIFA but failed, so it published the information online.

FIFA did not say exactly what data was taken or who is affected. It did not respond to questions about the nature of the incident.

title: Many people willing to pay to vanish from search results
text:
A US survey suggests many people are willing to pay to remove their personal details from public search results, driven by fears about what artificial intelligence can infer from scattered data.

A survey of 1,008 US adults by privacy company Incogni found that 55% would pay to have their personal information permanently removed from public search results. The same group found that 53% would like a record of everyone who has searched for their name over the past five years.

Darius Belejevas, Head of Incogni, said the main concern is no longer just what people can find, but what artificial intelligence (AI) can guess by connecting different pieces of information. He noted that an address, old workplace, or family connection might seem harmless alone, but together they can reveal patterns about a person’s life that they never intended to make public.

The survey also highlighted how common it is for people to check their own online presence. Just over half of respondents had searched for their own name in the past five years, often before job interviews, renting a home, or going on a date. This helps them understand what a hiring manager or potential partner might discover.

However, removing information is not simple. Data brokers and people-search sites compile details like home addresses and employment histories into searchable profiles. Incogni notes that adjusting social media privacy settings will not remove this information from these third-party websites.

title: Fix for Ghostscript flaw that lets files run commands
text:
A security fix is available for a flaw in Ghostscript that could let malicious files run commands on servers.

Ghostscript is a program that many web servers use to convert files like PDFs and images into other formats. It often runs in the background when you upload a file to a website.

Security firm pwn.ai showed that a specific type of file could escape the program's built-in safety checks. This allowed the file to run commands on the server that was processing it.

The flaw has now been patched. This means the makers have released a fix to stop this from happening.

If you run a website or server that uses Ghostscript, you should update the software to the latest version to protect it.

title: Windows update may stop printing for some business users
text:
Microsoft says a recent update can cause printing errors on some Windows 11 computers, but a fix is not yet available.

Microsoft has confirmed that some users are experiencing printing problems after installing a specific Windows update. This issue affects only computers running Windows 11 version 24H2 or later. The problem occurs when the update is installed alongside a security tool called Forcepoint DLP Endpoint Agent.

According to Microsoft, the print option may appear greyed out or show errors. This happens because the Print Spooler service, which manages print jobs, fails to start. Microsoft says this issue is linked to a compatibility problem between the update and the Forcepoint software.

A permanent fix is not yet available. However, Forcepoint has shared a temporary workaround for its customers. This can be found in a support document on the Forcepoint portal, which requires a sign-in to access.

These issues should not affect systems with the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, only those that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through Microsoft's Windows Autopatch, a cloud-based enterprise service designed to automate Windows and Microsoft 365 updates.

title: ScreenConnect flaw exploited to hijack technician computers
text:
A critical security flaw in ScreenConnect software is being exploited to target computers used by IT support staff.

Security researchers have found that threat actors are exploiting a serious weakness in ConnectWise ScreenConnect. This software is often used by IT support companies, known as managed service providers, to fix problems on other people's computers.

The flaw, called CVE-2026-84869, may allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorisation or host confirmation in certain circumstances. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) describes this as a critical issue, giving it the highest possible risk score of 9.9.

According to The Hacker News, threat actors are exploiting this weakness. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities in September 2026.

The good news is that a fix is available. The sources confirm that the flaw is now patched, meaning the software has been updated to stop this specific attack from working.

title: Microsoft confirms data breach in Entra Connect Health service
text:
Microsoft has fixed a flaw that let attackers view some business details, but says no passwords were stolen.

Microsoft has disclosed a data breach in its Entra Connect Health service. This is a cloud tool that helps company IT teams check if their identity systems are working correctly. The company said it found a weakness in the service on 9 November 2026. This flaw had been present since 23 July 2026.

Microsoft fixed the problem on 19 November 2026. It says the issue was fixed on its servers, so customers do not need to install any software updates. The company confirmed that no passwords, security tokens, or keys were stolen. However, attackers could view some business information, such as administrator email addresses and domain names.

Microsoft says this information could be used to send convincing fake messages, known as phishing. These messages might try to trick staff into giving away more details. The company has not said how many businesses were affected. It advises organisations to check their own records for any unusual activity.

title: Microsoft fixes security flaw in Azure API Management
text:
Norway's security agency says an actor was actively looking for business secrets in a flaw in Microsoft's cloud service.

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management service. This service helps businesses manage how their software talks to each other.

The NSM said an unknown actor was actively looking for access tokens and secrets in this system. Access tokens are digital keys that allow programs to connect to services securely. The agency noted that several Norwegian businesses, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, were affected.

The NSM stated it is still uncertain how the actor gained access.

title: Okta links new data leak site to ShinyHunters group
text:
Security firm Okta says a group linked to ShinyHunters may have rebranded as INCEPTION and is using voice calls to steal login details.

Okta’s Threat Intelligence team has identified a new threat cluster called O-UNC-053. The firm says this group is likely connected to the ShinyHunters extortion crew. It appears the group has rebranded itself under the name INCEPTION.

The group uses 'vishing' attacks. This is a type of voice phishing where criminals call you to trick you into giving away your login details. They may also ask you to approve requests on fake web pages.

Okta has linked this activity to a new data leak site called INCEPTION. A data leak site is a website where stolen information is often published or sold. The sources do not provide specific details on which companies or individuals have been targeted by this specific cluster.

title: VMware patches critical security flaw in vCenter
text:
Broadcom has released updates to fix a serious bug in VMware software that could let attackers bypass login checks.

Broadcom has shipped patches to fix 23 security flaws in its VMware products. This includes a critical bug in vCenter, a tool used to manage virtual machines. The flaw is rated 9.8 out of 10, which is very high. It sits in a part of the software called the VMware Directory Service, or vmdir.

The bug allows a bad actor to bypass authentication. Authentication is the process of proving who you are, usually with a password. If this flaw is used, an attacker could get into the system without proper permission.

The update covers several VMware tools, including ESX, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer. Broadcom has made the fixes available to address these issues. Users of these products need to install the new patches to close the gap.

title: Police disrupt 57 illegal streaming services
text:
Authorities from 11 countries have disrupted 57 illegal streaming services that drew over 7.3 million visits a year.

Police from 11 countries have worked together to disrupt 57 illegal streaming services. These services offered access to TV channels, live sports, and movies without permission from the copyright owners. They charged users a small monthly fee for this unauthorised access.

Europol, the EU’s law enforcement agency, said the operation identified 321 websites involved in the scheme. Investigators traced over €26 million in cryptocurrency transactions. Cryptocurrency is a digital form of money that can be hard to track. Experts from crypto companies helped follow the money to find the people behind the services.

The European Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance said legitimate providers lose around €4.83 billion a year. This is because roughly 60 million people in Europe use these illegal platforms. The joint action also involved the European Union Intellectual Property Office and INTERPOL.

This crackdown follows several other major operations in recent years. In June, a separate operation removed more than 27,000 illegal streaming links. In May, Italian authorities dismantled a piracy platform that gave illegal access to services like Netflix and Disney+.

title: Fake screenshot tool leads to Microsoft Store malware
text:
A fake download site tricked users into installing a malicious app from the genuine Microsoft Store, giving hackers control of their Windows PCs.

Security firm eSentire reported that a Windows user searching for a screenshot tool was redirected to a fake website. The site offered a file that looked like the official Snipping Tool. However, the installer actually pointed to a Microsoft Store app called Setup Assistant.

This app opened a backdoor and delivered malware known as Vinci RAT. This type of software, called a remote access trojan, allows criminals to run commands, place files, and launch other threats on an infected computer. The app also set up a hidden task to keep the malware running every 10 minutes.

The case is unusual because the app was listed on the real Microsoft Store, not a fake copy of the website. eSentire said Microsoft initially replied that the app did not violate its terms. The report does not say if Microsoft later removed the listing or how many other computers were affected.

title: Criminals use phone calls to steal cloud account details
text:
A security firm says criminals are calling businesses to trick staff into giving up access to their online accounts.

Palo Alto Networks, a security company, has reported a rise in phone-based scams. It says these attacks have been happening since August 2026. The criminals call people at work and use social engineering to trick them. Social engineering is a way of manipulating people into doing something they shouldn't.

The company says these calls have led to stolen data and attempts to demand money. The targets included businesses in the financial, healthcare, and legal sectors. The attacks affected companies in the US, the UK, and Australia. Other industries targeted included construction.

The security firm says it is tracking these 'waves' of attacks. It has also responded to them. The goal of the criminals is to hijack cloud accounts. A cloud account is an online login that lets you access files and services stored on the internet, rather than on a physical computer.

title: Fake Google Sheets extension steals Gmail messages
text:
A piece of malware is installing a fake Google Sheets add-on in Chrome to read Gmail messages from Windows computers.

Researchers at Gen Digital have identified a new feature in malware called Remus Stealer. It silently installs a fake Google Sheets extension in Google Chrome on Windows computers. This add-on runs in the background and reads new emails from users who are already signed in to Gmail.

The extension sends the sender, subject, and body of messages to an attacker-controlled server. It checks for unread mail roughly once a minute. Because it reads mail from inside the browser, it does not need to steal your login cookies to work. Researchers found no evidence that it uses a security flaw in Gmail itself.

You can spot this fake add-on by checking your Chrome extensions page. Look for a Google Sheets card marked as 'unpacked' and a Developer Mode switch that you did not turn on. The fake extension borrows the description of the legitimate Google Docs Offline tool but has no spreadsheet interface.

If you change your password while the extension is still installed, it can keep reading your mail using your new login. This makes the theft look like it survived a password reset. The malware developers claim it works even after users revoke their sessions, but researchers say you must remove the software to stop it.

title: Drupal websites being targeted by new security flaw
text:
A security hole in the popular website software Drupal is being used in attacks, so site owners need to update their systems now.

Security agency CISA and Drupal developers say a flaw in the software is being exploited in the wild. The issue, named Fail2Install, allows an attacker to take over a website or run harmful code. It was fixed on 18 November, but attacks started shortly after that date.

The problem affects the part of Drupal used to set up a new site. An attacker can use this to reinstall the software and hijack the website. Drupal has rated the vulnerability as 'highly critical' because of the attacks.

Patches are available in Drupal versions 11.4.13, 11.3.22 and 10.6.22. Older versions that are no longer supported will not get a fix. CISA added the flaw to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities on 24 November.

It is not clear how many websites are affected. There is no public information on specific attacks. This is the third time a Drupal flaw has been exploited in the wild this year.

title: Microsoft confirms login problems after November Windows updates
text:
New security updates for Windows are causing some users to fail to sign in to certain apps and devices.

Microsoft has confirmed that some customers are experiencing authentication issues after installing the November security updates. These updates were designed to fix a high-severity security flaw in the Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime. This flaw allowed attackers to run code on unpatched systems without user interaction.

The fix improves how Windows handles a type of login called NTLM. It makes these logins more secure by adding extra checks. However, Microsoft says this change can cause problems if third-party apps or devices do not handle the new security rules correctly. This includes some single sign-on solutions and authentication proxy servers.

Microsoft has not released a permanent fix for these login failures yet. The company advises users to check if their affected software or device supports a different, more secure login method called Kerberos. If it does not, users should contact the vendor for an update that works with the new Windows security requirements.

As a temporary workaround, Microsoft suggests changing a specific setting in the Windows registry. This allows older, less secure logins to work again. However, the company warns this is only a short-term solution and may be removed in future updates.

title: UK agency advises on stopping automated AI attacks
text:
The NCSC has published new guidance to help organisations defend against automated attacks from AI tools.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has shared advice to tackle a rise in automated attacks. These attacks use AI frameworks, such as ARTEX, to probe for weaknesses in digital systems.

The NCSC says these tools do not usually find new security flaws. Instead, they exploit common mistakes, such as weak passwords or settings that are left open by default. The agency notes that these attacks can be fast and intense.

The guidance suggests eight steps for security teams. These include checking what services are visible to the public and locking down access. It also recommends using strong login checks and monitoring for unusual activity to spot these automated tools early.

The NCSC advises that while AI defence is the future, basic security hygiene is the priority now. Organisations should follow established standards, such as Cyber Essentials, to build a strong foundation.

title: Ofcom proposes 48-hour limit for removing intimate images
text:
Ofcom is consulting on new rules that would force tech firms to remove non-consensual intimate images within 48 hours of a report.

Ofcom has published a consultation on strengthened industry codes. These rules would require platforms to remove non-consensual intimate images as quickly as possible. The maximum time allowed for removal would be 48 hours after a report is received.

The changes reflect recent updates to the law under the Crime and Policing Act 2026. Ofcom says these measures aim to protect women and girls from online harm. The regulator is inviting responses to the consultation by 20 January 2027.

Ofcom is also checking if companies are using 'hash matching' technology. This is a method that helps detect and prevent the upload of illegal images. Several services, including xHamster, have already started using this technology. Ofcom has opened two investigations into companies suspected of not complying with these duties.

From today, Ofcom is writing to over 1,000 services about their obligations. It is also publishing online resources to help these services understand what they need to do. The regulator says it will open further investigations if companies fall short of their duties.

title: Microsoft fixes blank screen bug blocking Office apps
text:
A recent update has fixed a problem that stopped some people from opening Word, Excel, and Outlook.

Microsoft has fixed a bug that prevented some users from accessing their Office applications. The issue caused a blank white box to appear on the screen. This box had no text or buttons and could not be closed.

According to Microsoft, this stopped people from using Outlook, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, and Access. One user reported installing three separate versions of 365 and launching applications in safe mode without success.

The company confirmed the fix is now available in Microsoft 365 Apps Version 2611 (Build 16.0.20625.20142), released last week. Customers who cannot update because of this bug can upgrade to the latest version from the command line.

This is the latest in a series of issues affecting Microsoft 365 users this year. Earlier bugs included problems with copying and pasting in Excel and errors that removed older versions of Office from some systems.

title: Adobe releases urgent fixes for critical security flaws
text:
Adobe has released updates to fix serious weaknesses in its software that could allow attackers to run harmful code on servers.

Adobe published security updates on 24 November 2026. These updates fix critical vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager and Adobe Campaign Classic. A vulnerability is a weakness in software that a hacker can use to break in.

The flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers. They could also allow attackers to gain permissions they should not have or bypass security checks. Adobe said it was not aware of any attacks using these flaws when it published the updates.

The updates are rated as critical, with a severity score of 9.9 out of 10. This high score indicates a serious risk. However, Adobe noted that no active exploitation was reported at the time of the release.

For businesses using these products, it is essential to install the latest updates. Adobe has provided specific version numbers and hotfixes for administrators to check. This ensures the software is protected against these specific weaknesses.

title: EU online course users' names and emails leaked in cyberattack
text:
The European Commission confirmed that a cyberattack exposed the names and email addresses of people who use its online learning platform.

The European Commission has confirmed that a cyberattack on its systems led to a data breach. The attack affected the EU Academy, an online platform where people outside the Commission can take courses about EU policies. The Commission said that names and email addresses of users were exposed. It is still investigating the full scale of the leak.

The Commission’s cybersecurity team detected the attack on 22 October. They identified a tool called ARTEX, which uses artificial intelligence to find weaknesses in computer systems, as a possible tool used in the attack. The Commission has suspended access to the EU Academy while the investigation continues. It has also notified the European Data Protection Supervisor.

Spokesman Thomas Regnier said the Commission is warning users about the risk of phishing. Phishing involves fake messages that try to trick you into giving away personal details. Because the attackers now have names and emails, scam messages may look more convincing. The Commission has not contacted individuals directly but posted a general warning on the website.

Some reports suggest the attack may be linked to a group backed by China, but the Commission has not officially confirmed who is responsible. The investigation is still ongoing, and the Commission says it will only name the attackers once the inquiry is complete.

title: Fake Minecraft add-on steals login details
text:
A fake Minecraft add-on is stealing player login details and installing hidden software on Windows computers.

Security researchers at SonicWall have identified a fake file called Farmutils-Loader.jar. It looks like a normal add-on for the game Minecraft, but it is actually malware. When a player opens the file, it steals their active login token. This token allows someone else to use the player's Minecraft services for up to 24 hours.

The file also downloads a hidden program called an infostealer. This tool is designed to steal other information from the computer. It hides itself inside what looks like a normal picture file. The malware can start just by double-clicking the file, even if the game is not running.

SonicWall says this file is part of a malware family called SilentNet. They have seen more than 1,200 samples of this family in the wild. The researchers could not confirm exactly what the second stage of the malware steals, as they did not recover the full file. However, it is designed to gather logs and data from the computer.

title: AI tool used to build fake login pages for Microsoft and Google
text:
Criminals used an AI website builder to create fake sign-in pages that looked like major brands, putting passwords at risk.

Security researchers at Aikido found 42 fake web pages on the Hugging Face platform. These pages copied the look of sign-in screens for 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, and Coinbase. The researchers say the pages were built using an AI tool called DeepSite.

The pages were found in October 2026. At the time, 34 were live and eight were paused. By the end of the month, all 42 pages were paused or no longer reachable. The researchers could not say how many people visited the pages or entered their details.

Some fake pages asked for one-time codes, card details, or personal information. One fake Microsoft page even sent visitors to the real Outlook site after collecting their data. This makes it hard for people to tell if they are on a safe page.

The risk came from the content hosted on the platform, not from visiting Hugging Face itself. The secure connection (HTTPS) on these pages did not prove that the brands owned them.

title: New 'Inception' gang uses phone calls to steal work logins
text:
A new criminal group is calling employees to trick them into giving up their work passwords, but no major companies have confirmed a breach yet.

A new data extortion group called 'Inception' has launched a large-scale campaign. It targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials, which are the master keys that let you log in to many different work apps with one password.

The group says it has stolen data from seven companies, including chip maker AMD and PepsiCo. However, none of these firms have publicly confirmed a data breach. Cybersecurity firm ReversingLabs says the group has been operating since late October.

The attacks rely on phone calls rather than emails. Callers pose as support staff and pressure employees to reset their passwords through fake sign-in pages. These pages look like official legal or security sites to trick users into typing in their details.

Security company Okta links this group to a previous gang called ShinyHunters. Okta says the group likely changed its name after members were arrested. The Inception group denies this link, claiming it operates independently.

title: Ofcom checks X's handling of illegal content and Grok changes
text:
Ofcom is monitoring X's response to hate and terror content and scrutinising data from its first quarterly report, while continuing its investigation into the Grok AI chatbot.

Ofcom, the UK's online safety regulator, has received X's first quarterly report on how it handles reports of illegal hate and terror content. The regulator says the data shows some improvements in how quickly X reviews these reports. However, Ofcom still has concerns about how effectively X removes this illegal material from its platform.

Ofcom is also continuing its investigation into X over the Grok AI chatbot. The chatbot was used to create and share demeaning sexual deepfakes of real people, including children, which may amount to illegal content. As a result of Ofcom's pressure, X has made changes to ensure that content labelled as pornography is consistently restricted for accounts that have not completed age assurance.

Separately, SpaceXAI, the company behind the standalone Grok service, has introduced new restrictions. It now blocks people with UK IP addresses from viewing, generating and/or sharing pornographic content using the image generation technology provided by standalone Grok. It has also implemented restrictions to its companion chatbots to prevent them from engaging in sexually explicit conversations with UK users.

Ofcom will continue to monitor these changes. It plans to publish a further analysis of X's performance in the new year once it has received more data from the company

title: Signal blocks screenshots on Apple and Google phones
text:
Signal is stopping screenshots by default on iPhones and Android phones to protect your messages from AI tools.

The messaging app Signal has announced it will stop users from taking screenshots of messages by default. This change applies to people using Apple and Google operating systems. It follows similar restrictions Signal put in place for Microsoft users last year.

Signal says this move is needed because of concerns about how tech giants use artificial intelligence. AI agents are tools that can scan what is on your screen to answer questions or perform tasks. Signal’s president, Meredith Whittaker, said these agents are making the environment "increasingly hostile to privacy".

Whittaker warned that these AI tools capture data and send it to servers outside of Signal’s control. This could put the privacy of everyone in a conversation at risk. She described the situation as an "existential threat" to the app's mission.

You can still take screenshots if you want to. You can turn off the block in the app’s settings. However, Signal warns that this fix is not perfect. It does not stop AI agents from accessing data in other ways, such as reading files already saved on your device.

title: US government urged to fix email security bug
text:
A flaw in a popular email filtering tool was used by hackers, prompting US officials to urge a fix before Thanksgiving.

The US cybersecurity agency, CISA, has warned federal departments to patch a security flaw in N-able’s Mail Assure platform. This software helps block spam and malware from reaching inboxes. The bug, known as CVE-2026-134624, has a high severity score of 9.3.

CISA added the issue to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on Monday evening. This means hackers have already used the bug to break into one of N-able’s servers. The agency urged US government bodies to install the fix by Thanksgiving.

N-able said it fixed the bug over the weekend and restored access for its customers. The company stated that email sending and spam filtering continued to work during the incident. It also said it found no evidence of the bug being used on any other servers.

N-able promised to publish a full report on what happened within two weeks. It clarified that this incident is not linked to other security issues in its N-central software, which was discussed recently.

title: ShinyHunters claims return after arrests
text:
A criminal group says it is back online after several members were reportedly arrested, but BleepingComputer noted that the keys used do not confirm identity.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned in posts on a new data leak site. This happened after a series of arrests over the past two months targeting alleged members. The new site launched on 23 November 2026 and contains messages in Russian and English. The group says it is returning after months of rumours and misinformation.

To prove they are the real group, the operators signed messages using old digital keys. These keys, known as PGP keys, are like digital signatures that verify a message comes from a specific person. BleepingComputer confirmed the new messages were signed with keys the group used in 2020. However, these keys were retired in March 2026 and have been shared with many people. So, they do not prove the same individuals are running the group now.

The group also mocked former members who were reportedly arrested. It mentioned a man detained in Jordan and a Canadian executive arrested in Pennsylvania. The statement says these people made 'silly mistakes' that led to their capture. The group claims it will now communicate only through a specific hacking forum and its new website.

BleepingComputer noted that it is unclear if this is the original group or imposters using old tools. The group says it will launch a new system for hosting stolen data. It will stop using its old backup server

title: VMware releases fixes for serious security flaws in ESX and vCenter
text:
Broadcom has released updates to fix 23 security weaknesses in VMware software, including critical issues that could allow attackers to run harmful code.

Broadcom announced on Tuesday that it has released patches for 23 vulnerabilities across several VMware products. These fixes address serious flaws in ESX and vCenter, which are tools used to manage virtual computers.

The vCenter updates fix seven bugs, including a critical issue that could let an attacker bypass security checks. The ESX updates fix seven other issues, including three critical weaknesses that could allow code to be executed on the main system. Broadcom explained that on some products, this could lead to code execution on the machine where the software is installed.

According to Broadcom, some of these issues were already fixed in a vCenter update released last week. Customers who installed that specific version do not need to update again. However, users of vCenter 9.1.x, ESX, VMware Tools, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer need to install the new updates.

Broadcom did not say if these flaws are currently being used by criminals. The company noted that it does not always warn about active exploitation in its public notices.

title: Security firm Radware says customer cloud keys exposed
text:
A cybersecurity company admits attackers accessed some customer details and cloud keys through a mistake in its internal system.

Radware, a company that helps protect websites from attacks, says it found a security problem on 19 November 2026. Attackers got into an internal tool that was accidentally left open to the public internet. This tool is called a Cloud WAF management API, which is a secure door for managing website protection settings.

Radware says the attackers could see some customer contact details. For a smaller group of customers, they also accessed keys used to send log files to cloud storage. These keys are like passwords that allow specific programs to talk to cloud services like Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure.

The company says it blocked the originating IP address and access to the internal management API. It also revoked and replaced all internal account credentials after detecting the breach on Thursday, ten hours after the initial unauthorized API access. It also says the main protection services for customers continued to work without interruption. Radware is still checking if the stolen keys were actually used to access any data.

The firm has asked affected customers to change their cloud storage keys immediately. It also advised them to check their cloud accounts for any signs of unusual activity since mid-November.

title: Turnitin confirms cyberattack on customer systems
text:
The education software firm says it detected unauthorised activity and is investigating with outside experts.

Turnitin has told users that it found unauthorised activity on some of its systems. The company says it has started its emergency response plan and is working with outside security specialists.

Turnitin is a well-known tool used by schools and universities to check student work for plagiarism and AI-generated text. Its CEO, Chris Caren, said in a public letter that law enforcement and cyber regulators have been notified.

The company says its systems are currently working normally and are safe to use. It also stated that the affected systems do not collect government ID details or financial information.

However, Turnitin has not said exactly what happened or if any user data was stolen. It is still monitoring its systems to make sure the threat is gone.

title: Microsoft testing fix for Windows 11 Bluetooth audio quality drops
text:
Microsoft is testing a fix for a long-standing issue that lowers audio quality when using Bluetooth headphones with a microphone.

Windows 11 has a known problem where audio quality drops when you use Bluetooth headphones. This happens because the computer switches to a lower-quality mode to handle the microphone. It often occurs when you join a voice chat or use voice typing.

Microsoft is now testing a fix for this. It is available in preview builds for the Beta and Experimental channels. The fix allows newer Bluetooth devices to keep playing high-quality stereo sound even while the microphone is active.

According to Microsoft, this works for devices that support a specific audio standard called LE Audio. It includes headphones, earbuds, and speakers that support 48kHz playback. Users can find the setting in their sound options to ensure the best quality.

title: Criminal uses AI to target European banks and councils
text:
A French-speaking cybercriminal used an AI tool to attack European organisations, showing how technology is changing online threats.

SOCRadar, a security research firm, has reported on a new cybercrime operation called BabidiGhost. The research says a French-speaking operator spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities.

The operator used a 'jailbroken' AI agent. This is an artificial intelligence tool that has been modified to ignore its safety rules. The criminal wrote simple, misspelled French instructions for the AI. The AI then performed the technical work of the attacks.

The research team says the operator left the complex parts of the hacking to the machine. This suggests that criminals may not need deep technical skills to launch attacks if they can direct an AI tool effectively.

This story highlights how AI is being used in cybercrime. It is important for organisations to stay vigilant, as the methods used by criminals are evolving.

title: GTA 6 hacker released on licence
text:
A man who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence, with a warning to not let it happen again.

A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence. The report notes that this sentence may not deter young people engaging in cybercrime. It suggests the outcome could be seen as a free pass by those considering similar offences.

title: GTA VI hacker gets seven-year sentence, released same day
text:
A British man who hacked Rockstar Games and leaked game footage was sentenced to prison but released immediately due to time already served.

Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced to seven years in prison for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking footage of Grand Theft Auto VI. He was released the same day because he had already spent time in a psychiatric hospital.

Kurtaj admitted to six offences, including four under the Computer Misuse Act. He carried out the hacks in 2022 while on bail for earlier crimes. Police said he used an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into a hotel television to break into the systems of Uber, Revolut, and Rockstar Games.

The judge reduced his initial nine-year sentence by two years. Kurtaj will now serve the rest of his sentence under supervision in the community. He can be returned to prison if he breaks the conditions of his release.

Police are applying for an order to restrict his activities. A five-year order has already been imposed, banning him from using the messaging apps Telegram and Discord.

title: UK cyber agency warns of rise in AI-assisted attacks
text:
The National Cyber Security Centre says attackers are using AI tools to find and exploit old security weaknesses faster.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has reported a marked rise in cyberattacks assisted by artificial intelligence since September. The agency says these attacks are not using new tricks. Instead, AI tools are helping criminals find and use existing security gaps much faster.

The NCSC notes that these tools make attacks cheaper and more persistent. However, the agency stresses that the weaknesses being exploited are not new. A forgotten password or an unprotected connection that might have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

The centre warns that AI does not make standard security practices obsolete. In fact, it says building strong foundations matters more than ever. The NCSC states that nearly everything it has seen can be prevented by following basic cyber security best practice.

title: US state shuts down myColorado app after data breach
text:
The myColorado app is offline while officials investigate a breach that may have exposed data for up to 150,000 people.

The myColorado app is currently offline. This follows a data breach where an unauthorised user accessed information on the platform. The app belongs to the US state of Colorado.

Officials found the problem on 18 November. The Governor’s Office of Information Technology confirmed that someone had gained unauthorised access to the data. The app will remain shut down while the investigation continues.

Up to 150,000 people may be affected by this breach. The exact number of people whose details were seen is not yet known. Officials are working to understand the full scale of the incident.

title: Billions of passwords exposed in two database leaks
text:
Two separate online databases left billions of usernames and passwords open to the public, according to new findings.

Researchers found two unrelated databases. These databases held over 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, and national identity numbers.

The data was left exposed to anyone on the internet. The findings were shared with WIRED magazine.

The leaks included documents and personal information. It is not yet clear exactly which services these databases belonged to. The reports describe the scale of the exposure rather than the specific cause.

title: Hong Kong hospital pauses app after data breach
text:
A hospital in Hong Kong has paused its patient app after finding that personal details were accessed without permission.

Gleneagles Hospital in Hong Kong has stopped using its patient mobile app. The hospital said it found unauthorised activity on 18 November. This involved the security systems that support the app called My Gleneagles.

The hospital stated that personal data was accessed without permission. This included patients' names, identity document numbers, and contact details.

The hospital posted a statement on its website on Tuesday. It confirmed the detection of the unauthorised access. No further details were provided in the source material.

title: AI tools used to attack security servers in UK and US
text:
A criminal group is using AI tools to attack security servers used by major UK and global organisations.

Security firm GreyNoise says a criminal group is using AI-powered tools to attack Check Point Security Management servers. These servers are used by large organisations to manage their network security.

The group, tracked as GT13, targeted at least 22 organisations in the UK, US, and other countries. The sectors include energy, finance, government, and manufacturing. GreyNoise says the campaign started in early October and may still be ongoing.

The attackers used AI to find weak points in systems and exploit them automatically. They also used manual methods to gain control. GreyNoise says the group accessed servers from 99 different internet addresses, many of which were temporary or compromised devices.

The attackers stole data and moved between different systems. They used one victim’s server as a base to send commands to other compromised servers. GreyNoise confirmed activity between 17 October and 2 November, but believes the threat continues.

title: Donation platform breach exposes donor details
text:
A cyberattack on a fundraising software provider leaked personal details of donors to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

The Carnegie Endowment for International Peace says some donors had their information leaked due to a cyberattack on a third-party vendor called Soapbox Engage. The organisation sent emails to past donors on Friday to warn them about the breach. It said the incident happened on 28 October and that the attackers were removed from the system on 30 October.

Soapbox Engage is an online fundraising platform used by charities. The Carnegie Endowment uses it for online donations. According to the organisation, the hackers stole names, email addresses, phone numbers and giving history. A spokesperson said no full credit card numbers were exposed.

The Carnegie Endowment hired a cybersecurity firm to confirm the attackers were removed. The organisation notified everyone in its database because of European data privacy laws. It did not say how many people were affected.

This incident happened at the same time as other fundraising platforms reported security issues. GoFundMe said it identified a cybersecurity incident where hackers breached its systems in two separate attacks in October and November. It said it has disabled unauthorised accounts and is monitoring for further suspicious activity.

title: US lawmakers warn ID check firms after massive data leak
text:
A group of US politicians has written to identity verification companies after a breach exposed millions of ID scans, raising fears about how your personal details are stored.

A bipartisan group of US federal lawmakers sent a letter to several identity verification companies on Monday. They are asking these firms to explain how they protect sensitive customer data. The letter cites a breach at a company called IDScan that happened in September.

According to the letter, the breach led to scans of more than 150 million people’s drivers’ licenses and other ID documents appearing for sale on the dark web. The dark web is a hidden part of the internet where illegal goods are often traded. The stolen data included detailed images, such as ultraviolet and infrared scans, which make the documents harder to fake.

The lawmakers said the breach also exposed nearly 600,000 medical cards and employment authorisations. They warned that foreign adversaries could use this commercial data to infer the behaviour of Americans. The letter urged companies to limit how much personal information they collect and store to reduce the risk of future hacks.

Independent journalist Brian Krebs, who first reported the breach, said he has found more than two dozen identity verification companies that store scanned IDs by default. He noted that customers often have to pay extra to stop these scans from being kept after the check is done.

title: McDonald's Japan app breach exposes customer location data
text:
McDonald's Japan confirmed a data breach affecting its app users, revealing purchase histories and location details, though no names or credit card numbers were stolen.

McDonald's Japan has confirmed that attackers accessed a database linked to its official smartphone app. The company said the exposed information includes customers' product purchase history, IP addresses, and mobile device location data.
