The fast-food chain stated that names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, and credit card details were not part of the breach. It also noted that the internal customer IDs exposed cannot be used on their own to identify specific individuals.

McDonald's Japan said it is working to invalidate the access credentials used in the attack and has reported the incident to Japan's data protection authorities. The company added that it has not detected any misuse of the app or services as a result of the incident.

This breach follows a wave of cyberattacks on Japanese companies this year. Last month, Burger King Japan also disclosed a major data breach affecting millions of customer records.

title: Latvian telecom firm leaves 125 million SMS messages exposed
text:
A database containing over 125 million text messages from a Latvian telecom provider was left open to the public.

CSC Telecom, a telecommunications provider in Latvia, left a database exposed. It contained more than 125 million SMS messages.

The records cover messages sent between October 2022 and September 2026.

The leak reportedly includes details for clients of several major companies. These include Swedbank, SEB, and airBaltic, along with dozens of other organisations.

title: Ofcom steps up checks to protect phone and broadband customers
text:
The UK regulator is working harder to ensure providers treat customers fairly, from fixing price hikes to making complaints easier to handle.

Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, has updated how it oversees phone and broadband providers. It is now engaging with a wider range of companies, including newer entrants, to check they follow the rules.

In the last 18 months, Ofcom has secured several changes. It made sure O2 corrected information about price rises for customers still in contract. It also worked with 10 providers to make it easier for customers to raise complaints and understand what happens next.

The regulator has also made early termination charges clearer. This means customers cancelling within their minimum contract term are less likely to be overcharged. Ofcom also stopped two smaller providers from automatically adding extras, like anti-virus software, during online sales.

If a provider does not improve after initial talks, Ofcom can take formal action. In July 2026, it fined Virgin Media £28 million because customers struggled to cancel their broadband services.

title: AI service providers found to have had customer prompts stolen
text:
Security firm Dragos says evidence indicates that at least three AI services appear to have been hacked, with customer prompts stolen without the companies knowing.

Cybersecurity firm Dragos says it discovered that at least three AI inference providers were breached. These companies host AI models and sell access to them. Dragos claims the intrusions were not detected until the firm notified the providers.

To find the leaks, Dragos sent about two million test messages to various AI services between July and November. These messages contained unique, trackable bait, such as fake web addresses and security keys. The firm then monitored the internet to see if anyone used this bait, which would prove the data had been stolen.

Dragos found evidence that attackers stole information from one of the tested providers. The firm’s chief research officer, HD Moore, said that because the test messages were processed alongside real customer requests, those real requests were “almost certainly copied too.” The biggest breach involved roughly 200 test keys stolen in late October.

OpenRouter, a service that connects users to many AI providers, said its own systems were not breached. However, it removed three unnamed providers in response to the incident. Other affected companies include Phala, Together AI, Novita, and Atlas Cloud.

title: Cyberattack disrupts hospital systems in Guadeloupe
text:
A cyberattack has forced a hospital in the French overseas department of Guadeloupe to delay non-emergency procedures.

A major cyberattack hit the university hospital in Guadeloupe on Saturday night. The attack disrupted the hospital's information systems and telephone lines.

Staff were unable to access several applications and databases. This forced the hospital to activate its emergency response plan. As a result, non-emergency procedures have been postponed.

The incident was reported by RFI.

title: Email security firm N-able fixes flaw after cyberattack
text:
N-able has patched a critical security flaw in its email services after a cyberattack disrupted access for some users.

N-able, a company that provides email security tools, confirmed that its Mail Assure and SpamExperts services were targeted in a cyberattack. The company said the attackers accessed a web server and likely reached certain credentials stored there. As a result, N-able temporarily disabled access to its management portal and other features to contain the incident.

During its investigation, the company found a critical vulnerability. This is a weakness in the software that allowed an authorised user to make the server connect to internal systems it should not have reached. N-able has now released a fix for this issue. The company states that the attack was limited to one specific server and that email delivery was not affected during the disruption.

Access to the services was restored on 21 November. N-able says it has found no evidence of further malicious activity since the fix was applied. The company is continuing its investigation and plans to share a detailed report on what happened within the next two weeks.

title: Microsoft fixes flaw that let attackers steal cloud keys
text:
Microsoft has fixed a security gap in its Azure cloud service that allowed attackers to steal secret codes used to connect different software.

Microsoft says it found a problem in a part of its Azure cloud service called API Management. This service helps organisations manage how their different apps talk to each other. The company says it fixed the issue on 19 November 2026.

Norwegian security officials linked this flaw to attacks on energy companies in Norway. They said the attackers tried to steal secret codes, known as credentials, that allow access to sensitive systems. Microsoft confirmed that some of these codes may have been exposed before the fix was put in place.

Microsoft told customers that the fix was applied automatically to their systems. However, the company warned that this does not cancel any codes that might have already been stolen. If an attacker has your codes, they can still use them to try to get into your systems.

Microsoft advised customers to change their secret codes immediately. It also suggested checking their system logs for any signs of unusual activity that might indicate someone else has been logging in.

title: South Korea power firm KEPCO confirms breach of 1.5 million records
text:
A major South Korean electricity company says its systems were hacked, exposing the personal and financial details of over 1.5 million people.

Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) has confirmed that an unauthorised user accessed its internal network. The company detected the breach on 20 November 2026. It quickly blocked outside access and suspended the affected services to stop further damage.

The breach affected three groups of people. Details for 650,487 customers were exposed, including names, addresses, bank account numbers, and card details. Information for 426,827 company representatives and 442,934 employees was also accessed. This included names, ID information, and contact details.

KEPCO says the attack used "advanced technologies such as AI" but did not give specific details on how the hacker got in. A threat actor using the alias "Noiem" has claimed responsibility on a hacker forum. However, authorities have not yet confirmed this attribution. The company is working with government and financial bodies to prevent misuse of the data.

The company is notifying affected individuals directly. It has also filed a report with data protection authorities. KEPCO warns that the exposed data could be used for targeted phishing. Phishing involves fake messages that try to trick you into giving away your details.

title: US spy agency back to normal after internal network crash
text:
The US National Security Agency has returned to normal operations after a software update caused its internal network to fail for several days.

The National Security Agency (NSA) says it is now operating under normal conditions. This follows a week when its internal communications network, called NSANet, crashed for much of the time.

The disruptions were caused by maintenance work on PHP, a common programming language used to build websites and apps. An NSA spokesperson confirmed the agency is back to business as usual, though some facilities are still running with limited staff.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the patches caused some systems to fail to restart as expected. He added that the problems were not caused by a cyberattack. Officials also said the issues were not connected to recent IT problems affecting Microsoft products or airline services.

title: US retailer The Container Store hit by cyberattack
text:
A US home goods retailer has restored its online systems after a cyberattack forced it to pause digital ordering.

The Container Store, a US-based retailer with about 100 stores, said it is recovering from a cyberattack. The incident forced the company to shut down its online ordering systems and limit in-store transaction processing. Its parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, confirmed that the website and systems have now been restored.

During the disruption, stores remained open but had to use alternative methods to process transactions. The company said it hired cybersecurity experts to contain the incident and restore the affected systems. It added that the incident only impacted The Container Store and did not affect its other brands, such as Bed Bath & Beyond.

A cybercriminal group called n0n listed the company on its leak site earlier this month. The company has not yet addressed these claims. So far, it does not appear that customer financial data was stolen, but the firm has not confirmed this definitively.

Cybersecurity experts say the n0n group specialises in ransomware and data extortion. They have attacked more than 100 organisations and demanded large sums of money. The group has primarily targeted healthcare and pharmaceuticals but recently claimed to have data from retail firms.

title: BADBOX botnet returns with record ad fraud
text:
A large network of infected Android devices is sending billions of fake ad requests daily, according to security researchers.

Security firm HUMAN says the BADBOX botnet has returned after being disrupted last year. It is now generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests every day. These requests come from infected Android-based devices, such as phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes.

The malware plays video ads in hidden windows to trick advertisers into paying for views that never happened. It also uses your device to hide other illegal traffic, making it look like it is coming from a normal home connection. HUMAN says this new version is more than three times larger than the previous record holder.

Researchers linked the malware to a specific Chinese electronics manufacturer. The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns.

HUMAN and Google have taken down some of the control servers and removed apps that spread the malware. However, HUMAN warns the operators will likely adapt and try to rebuild the network again.

title: FBI investigating apparent hack of national crime database
text:
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking into a suspected breach of its main criminal justice database, though the full scale of the issue is not yet clear.

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, or NCIC. This is a computerised database that holds criminal justice records, such as details on fugitives, missing persons, and stolen property. It is used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies.

A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that the FBI is looking into the incident. The FBI declined to comment on the apparent hack. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear.

President Donald Trump said in an interview that he had just heard about it and that it was "not good". This news comes as the US has seen a series of digital outages in government and private sectors. Officials have said those outages were caused by routine system upgrades, not cyberattacks. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.

title: Austrian Foreign Ministry website hacked, staff details accessed
text:
Hackers accessed the names and contact details of diplomats at the Austrian Foreign Ministry, though no public data was stolen.

Austria's Foreign Ministry said hackers breached one of its websites between 12 and 13 November. The breach affected a site run by an external service provider. The ministry confirmed that the names and official contact information of employees in Vienna and abroad were accessed.

The ministry said the breach has been contained. It stated that no personal information belonging to members of the public was compromised. It is not yet clear how the hackers gained access or if they stole any other information.

The incident happened around the same time as a global Microsoft service outage. Microsoft said that outage was caused by a software bug. Austrian authorities have not established whether the two events are connected.

A ministry spokesperson said the incident is being taken "very seriously". They noted that the attack has not been attributed to any specific group. The ministry has notified Austria's cybersecurity and data protection authorities.

title: Bromcom breach exposes school staff and pupil emails
text:
A UK education software provider confirmed that email addresses for 355k people were exposed in a September 2026 data breach.

In September 2026, Bromcom, a UK education software provider, suffered a data breach. The incident involved a legacy single sign-on registration system. Single sign-on is a way to use one set of login details for multiple services.

Bromcom confirmed that 355k unique email addresses were exposed. These belonged to staff and pupils at UK schools. The company also said that registration reference numbers were leaked.

However, Bromcom stated that no passwords or security tokens were exposed. The company confirmed the incident did not allow access to Microsoft or Google accounts. It also did not enable access to its school management system.

The breach was added to the Have I Been Pwned database on 23 November 2026. This site helps people check if their details have been leaked in past incidents.

title: Cisco video system flaw being used in attacks
text:
US security officials say criminals are using a serious flaw in Cisco video calling equipment to break into networks.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned that attackers are actively using a security flaw in Cisco Expressway devices. These are specialised machines that help companies connect their internal video calling systems to the internet securely.

Cisco released a fix for this issue in late October. However, CISA has now added the flaw to its list of vulnerabilities being used in real-world attacks. The agency told US government departments to install the update within three days.

A Russian security company called F6 said it saw attackers use this flaw to gain full control of devices connected to the internet. Once inside, the attackers tried to move around the network to steal sensitive information. CISA has urged all organisations, including private companies, to patch their systems quickly to stop these attacks.

title: Call centre operator jailed for scamming 30,000 Americans
text:
A Peruvian call centre operator was sentenced to eight years in prison for helping steal millions of dollars from over 30,000 Spanish-speaking US residents in a years-long government-impersonation fraud scheme.

Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza, a 45-year-old from Lima, Peru, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. She was sentenced to eight years in prison for her role in a large-scale fraud scheme. The Department of Justice said the scheme defrauded more than 30,000 Spanish-speaking residents of the United States out of $15 million.

The scammers first contacted victims claiming they qualified for free services or products. They then impersonated US government officials and lawyers. They told victims they were contractually obligated to pay large sums to receive the services.

According to court documents, Alcedo managed and operated Peruvian call centres between January 2013 and December 2018. She and her accomplices threatened victims with court action, arrest, and immigration consequences. The US Attorney said the criminals used fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars.

This case follows a June 2026 warning from the US Federal Trade Commission. It stated that Americans lost $3.5 billion to impersonation scams in 2025. Approximately $920 million of that was stolen by government impersonators.

title: Tower Records says 11 million customer records may have been leaked
text:
A Japanese music retailer says a cyberattack may have exposed personal details for millions of customers, though it claims no credit card data was taken.

Tower Records, a Japanese music retailer, has announced that a cyberattack on 19 November 2026 may have compromised approximately 11 million customer records. The company stated that the leaked data includes personal details such as names, dates of birth, and delivery addresses. However, Tower Records said that no credit card information was included in the breach.

The company made this announcement following reports in Japan about the incident. It is important to note that these figures are based on the company's own assessment of the damage. There is no further information yet on how the attackers gained access to the system or what they did with the data.

If you have an account with Tower Records, you should check your email for any official notices from the company. They may provide specific advice on how to protect your account or what steps to take next. Keep an eye on your bank statements for any unusual activity, although the company says card details were not leaked.

title: Samsung Securities data breach exposes customer details
text:
Personal details for 8,241 customers have been exposed online.

South Korean firm Samsung Securities has suffered a data breach. The incident affected 8,241 customers. Personal information, including names, home addresses, and account numbers, was exposed online.

Times Now News reports that cyberattacks are rising globally. It notes that companies are finding it difficult to keep customer data safe thanks to AI.

title: Norway says hackers used Microsoft flaw to target energy firms
text:
Norwegian authorities say hackers exploited a security weakness in Microsoft's cloud service to try to steal sensitive details from energy companies.

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) says an unidentified group of hackers has been using a security flaw in Microsoft's cloud service to target sensitive information. The service, called Azure API Management, helps organisations manage connections between their different computer systems.

Two major Norwegian energy companies, Equinor and Skagerak Energi, reported cyberattacks last week. Equinor said it detected the attack on Tuesday but did not fully stop it until Friday. The company added that there is no sign that data was stolen or changed, and that its oil and gas production continued normally.

Microsoft told Recorded Future News that it found the issue on 18 November and fixed it the next day. The company warned that hackers may have accessed passwords and other sensitive information stored in the vulnerable systems before the fix was applied. Microsoft said the problem mainly affected customers who had not followed its security advice or who stored sensitive data directly in the service instead of using a separate, more secure tool called Azure Key Vault.

Norwegian officials say the vulnerability affected organisations in several sectors, both in Norway and abroad. Martin Albert-Hoff, the director of operational cybersecurity at NSM, said it remains unclear how widely the flaw has been used. He warned that more

title: Gift card firm GlobeTopper hit by cyberattack
text:
A business that sells digital gift cards to other companies suffered a cyberattack, leading to lost revenue and redeemed cards.

GlobeTopper is a company that helps other businesses sell digital gift cards. It works with over 4,000 brands in 65 countries, including IKEA, Adidas, and Spotify. A cyberattack disrupted its operations in late October 2026.

The parent company, iQSTEL, said the attack was detected on 22 October. The company quickly shut down its platform to investigate. It took until 31 October to rebuild the system and restore services in stages from 1 November.

The attackers redeemed digital gift cards worth $70,000. GlobeTopper says it cannot recover these cards and will have to absorb the loss. The attack also caused an estimated $2.5 million in lost revenue for the company.

The company says the attackers got hold of certain access keys used by its business customers. These keys have been cancelled and replaced. An investigation is ongoing to check if any other personal or payment data was accessed.

title: Spanish football league LaLiga confirms data breach
text:
Personal details of fans using LaLiga's digital services were stolen in a cyberattack, and the organisation is now working to inform affected people.

LaLiga, the body that runs Spain's top men's professional football leagues, has confirmed a data breach. The organisation says a cybercriminal gained unauthorised access to one of its technology platforms between 14 and 16 November 2026.

According to LaLiga, the attacker extracted personal data belonging to users registered for digital services offered by LaLiga and some affiliated clubs. The incident was limited to this specific platform and did not affect other systems used to run the competitions.

On 16 November, LaLiga's security team identified the source of the access and took steps to block the attack. The organisation has reported the incident to the Spanish Data Protection Agency and the National Police's Central Cybercrime Unit.

LaLiga is coordinating with impacted clubs to inform affected fans. At the time of writing, no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack.

title: Email security firm N-able hit by cyberattack
text:
A cyberattack caused a multi-day outage for N-able's email filtering services, though the company says customer data was not compromised.

N-able, a provider of email security services, experienced a major disruption to its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services. The issue began on 16 November 2026 and affected customers across the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and Europe.

Initially, the company blamed the problem on technical configuration issues. However, on 18 November, N-able confirmed that a cyberattack was the cause. The company said it found no evidence that customer data or mailboxes were accessed by the attackers.

During the outage, email delivery and spam filtering continued to work. However, users could not access the management dashboard, view quarantined messages, or make changes to their settings. N-able has since taken steps to secure its systems and is working to restore full access to its tools.

The company stated that this incident is unrelated to a separate security issue affecting its N-central platform. It has provided specific guidance to customers based on how they use its services and continues to investigate the breach.

title: AI tool used to find flaw in medical imaging software
text:
Amazon says Chinese hackers used an AI tool to find a security gap in a medical imaging app, showing how fast automated attacks can now happen.

Amazon’s security team found a server left open to the public. It showed the history of an AI tool called Cairn being used by attackers. The tool is designed to help test computer systems for weaknesses.

The attackers told the AI to “obtain shell access” to university servers in East Asia. The AI tried many ways to break in, including guessing passwords. Most attempts failed, but one succeeded.

The AI found a flaw in an open-source medical imaging application called MONAI Label. This flaw allowed the AI to control the server. Amazon says the flaw was a “zero-day”, meaning it was unknown to the software makers before this attack.

The software makers fixed the bug on 18 November 2026. Amazon worked with a government partner to warn the affected universities. The attackers did not name the specific universities or countries involved.

title: GL.iNet routers and KVM devices hit by cloud flaw
text:
Hackers used a flaw in GL.iNet's remote management service to install malware on some home routers and remote control devices.

GL.iNet confirmed on 20 November 2026 that an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in its GoodCloud platform. This platform allows users to manage their routers and KVM devices remotely. The company said it has fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in the incident.

However, the fix does not remove malware from devices that were already infected. GL.iNet says stable firmware updates containing additional security fixes are scheduled for release on 22 November 2026. The company recommends that customers install the latest security firmware for their specific model, even if they do not see signs of infection.

Security researchers found custom malware on affected devices. This malware included reverse shells, which are tools that allow remote attackers to execute commands on infected devices. Some devices were also found with backdoors that could give attackers ongoing access.

It is not yet clear how many customers were impacted or if information was stolen. GL.iNet is investigating whether computers connected to infected KVM devices may have been compromised. The company has linked to a community-developed tool that can help scan for and remove known malware components.

title: US police database reportedly breached
text:
US police databases may have been hacked.

US news agencies report that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating a security breach. The incident reportedly targeted the National Crime Information Center (NCIC). This is a database used by US police to share details about wanted people and missing items.

The FBI has not confirmed the breach or said what information was accessed. It is also unclear how the attackers got in or if any data was stolen. The incident happened just two months after a previous attack on the FBI's recruitment website.

There is no evidence that this breach is connected to the earlier attack. The FBI is currently looking into the matter, but officials have not released further details. The US government has faced several cyber incidents this year, but this specific event involves US law enforcement systems.

title: AI agents used to hack medical image software
text:
Amazon says AI tools helped a China-linked group find and exploit a security flaw in a medical imaging tool.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team says it found evidence of a China-linked group using AI agents to attack medical software. The group targeted universities in East Asia, excluding mainland China. The software, called MONAI Label, helps doctors label medical images using AI.

The attackers used AI to find a bug in the software that allowed them to write files to the server. Amazon says this happened in about 11 minutes. The group then used this access to control other devices on the network. Amazon attributes the attack to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence.

The developers of MONAI Label have published an advisory. They rate the bug as critical. It affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. A fix is available in the next release. The software is open source, meaning anyone can download and use it.

title: Teenager held for trying to sell private data of 4,000 Agniveers
text:
A 14-year-old boy in India has been detained after allegedly stealing personal details from a government website.

Investigators in India say a 14-year-old boy gained unauthorised access to a test website. This site was designed for former Agniveers, a specific group of soldiers, to register for job opportunities in other government departments.

According to the reports, the boy allegedly extracted personal information from the site. He then posted an advertisement on the dark web, claiming he had the private data of 4,000 Agniveers.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet where illegal activities often take place. The boy is now being held by investigators for this alleged offence.

title: Scammers stole £3.7bn in 2026, says Which?
text:
Report Fraud recorded over 840,000 scam reports in the 13 months to the end of October 2026.

Which? says scammers have not slowed down this year. The national fraud reporting body, Report Fraud, recorded more than 840,000 reports in the 13 months to the end of October. In total, scammers stole £3.7bn this year.

The government introduced a Fraud Strategy at the start of the year. It focused on sharing intelligence but did not address the responsibility of tech companies for allowing scammers to target people. Which? notes that the Online Safety Act, which made platforms responsible for removing harmful content, has not yet led to material change.

Scammers often use pressure tactics, such as countdown timers on websites. They may also offer prices that seem too good to be true. Vague contact details, like a retailer having no physical address, are also warning signs.

title: VMware fixes critical flaw used in attacks
text:
Broadcom has released an urgent update to fix a security hole in VMware vCenter that hackers have been using since September.

Broadcom has released security updates to fix a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication bypass vulnerability that Chinese-linked hackers have exploited in zero-day attacks since September 2026. This vulnerability affects the VMware Directory Service in vCenter Server, a management platform organisations use to manage VMware virtualised environments.

According to reports from security researchers at Google, a hacking group linked to China has been using this flaw since early September 2026. The group, known as Armory Castle, used the bug to bypass authentication and gain unauthorised access. They then moved deeper into the networks to steal sensitive data.

Broadcom says the fix is available now and considers this an emergency update. The company advises organisations to install the patch as soon as possible. There are no official workarounds, though using network restrictions and firewalls can help reduce the risk while you wait for the update.

title: US firm says hackers stole data of 2m Japanese patients
text:
A US medical services company says hackers stole personal and medical data from over two million people in Japan.

SBC Medical Group Holdings, a US-based company that manages clinics, has disclosed a data breach. The company said hackers accessed an online platform it manages and stole data from databases linked to clinics in Japan.

According to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the attackers took basic details such as names, addresses, and dates of birth for 1,624,000 people. They also stole medical treatment descriptions and review text for thousands of others. SBC Medical Group said 14 people had credit card details stolen, but the company confirmed these cards were expired and could not be used for payments.

The company also reported that customer passwords and employee records were compromised. In a separate incident, hackers accessed a third-party booking service called Tribeau, affecting around 19,000 people. SBC Medical Group said it has isolated the affected servers and changed passwords to stop the attackers.

The company is still investigating the full impact on its business. It has not said how the hackers got in or if the data has been shared publicly.

title: Chase, Visa and Mastercard confirm data breach at third-party firm
text:
A cyberattack on a data analytics company may have exposed some customer names and email addresses, but no card numbers were stolen.

J.P. Morgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard have confirmed that a cyberattack at a third-party service provider exposed some customer information. The bank said the incident did not disrupt its services and is unrelated to other recent outages.

The n0n ransomware group claims it stole data from Qubole, a cloud data analytics company. The group says it accessed customer files between 14 and 26 October 2026. It alleges it stole contracts, pricing records and staff information.

Visa stated that its systems were not involved and no payment data, such as card numbers, were affected. Mastercard said the exposure involved a limited amount of email addresses from a small subset of cardholders in a specific benefit program.

Both companies say their payment networks are working normally. Mastercard added that the exposure has been contained and they are working with the provider to support affected cardholders.

title: Music distributor Too Lost data breach
text:
An unauthorised party claims to have obtained data from the music distributor for independent artists, Too Lost.

In November 2026, an unauthorised party claimed to have obtained data from Too Lost. This is a music distributor for independent artists. The data contained 724k unique email addresses belonging to artists, their collaborators and fans.

According to Have I Been Pwned, the stolen records may contain names, dates of birth, and physical addresses. Some records also contained bcrypt password hashes. A small subset included partial credit card data, identity verification information, such as passport, driver's licence or national ID numbers, and payouts made to artists.

Too Lost advised that its investigation remains ongoing. The company has engaged external forensic specialists to look into the incident. It has also taken measures to secure affected systems and credentials. The firm is working with advisors to coordinate communications and support for affected individuals.

title: Signal blocks AI assistants from reading your chats
text:
Signal has added new protections to stop built-in AI tools from capturing your private messages on iPhone and Android.

Signal has announced new security features for its messaging app. These updates stop AI assistants, such as Siri on iPhones and Gemini on Android phones, from reading your conversations while they perform tasks.

Signal’s president, Meredith Whittaker, said these AI tools can capture chat content as it appears on the screen. This puts private data outside of Signal’s control and exposes everyone in the conversation. The company spent months designing these protections to block the ways AI systems access app data.

However, Signal warns that AI agents might still find other ways to access your chats. This is a particular concern on Mac computers, where Signal currently cannot block screenshots. For Mac users, the company advises adding Signal to the 'Excluded Apps' list in your system settings to stop Siri from accessing your messages.

Signal has asked Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide clear documentation on how AI accesses data. This would allow app developers to easily opt out of AI access to screens and files. The company says these new protections are automatically activated when possible.

title: New rules force apps to fight child abuse images harder
text:
Ofcom has announced stricter rules requiring online platforms to use better tools to find and remove child sexual abuse material.

Ofcom, the UK’s online safety regulator, has set out new rules for websites and apps. These platforms must take stronger action to stop child sexual abuse material (CSAM) from being shared. The new measures come into force in early 2027, subject to parliamentary approval.

The rules require platforms to ban users who create or share this content. They must also use a method called 'hash matching' to find known illegal images. Hash matching is a way of identifying files by their digital fingerprint, so the same image can be spotted on different sites. This will be used on more sites, including pornography websites.

Ofcom also wants platforms to use automated tools to find new, previously unknown images. This will apply to file sharing services and the biggest social media platforms. The regulator says the scale of this problem is getting worse, partly because of artificial intelligence (AI) tools that can create fake images.

Oliver Griffiths, Ofcom’s Online Safety Group Director, said the current efforts by companies are not enough. He warned that firms that do not follow these new rules should expect to face serious consequences. The NSPCC, a children's charity, welcomed the move, noting that police data shows an average of 100 child sexual abuse image crimes happen in the UK every day.

title: Snapchat turns off 'Find Friends' for children by default
text:
Ofcom says Snapchat is changing its settings to better protect UK children from online strangers.

Ofcom has confirmed that Snapchat is now turning off its 'Find Friends' feature for child users by default. This means children will be better protected from stranger danger online.

Oliver Griffiths, Ofcom’s Online Safety Group Director, described this as an important and welcome improvement. He noted that the change is long overdue and that Ofcom will hold the company to account to ensure the rollout is completed this month.

Snapchat has also told Ofcom that highly effective age checks will be applied by the end of this year. This will ensure that all under-18s benefit from these new safety measures. Ofcom says it will monitor this progress closely.

The regulator sent a clear message to tech companies: tackling the risks of grooming to children is a non-negotiable. Companies that fail to step up to the mark will face enforcement action.

title: Stranger danger is top worry for parents of online gamers
text:
New Ofcom research shows talking to strangers is the biggest concern for parents, with over half of children playing with people they have never met.

Ofcom has published a new report highlighting that 'stranger danger' is the primary worry for parents of children who game online. Almost two-thirds of parents are concerned about their child talking to strangers through games or chat functions.

This concern is well-founded, as more than half of children who game online say they play with people they have never met in person. One in five children do this all or most of the time they play. This worry ranks higher than concerns about bullying, inappropriate content, or pressure to buy items in games.

While most parents set rules about how long their children can play, fewer than half set rules about who they can interact with. Ofcom notes that gaming is now a daily part of childhood for almost nine in ten children aged three to 17.

To help families this half term, Ofcom is encouraging parents to use a simple three-step approach: Check, Chat, and Change. This involves reviewing game settings, talking openly with children about their gaming experiences, and making adjustments to safety features where needed.

title: Windows 11 gets November update with search and face login fixes
text:
Microsoft has released an optional update for Windows 11 that improves search speed and helps facial recognition work in dark rooms.

Microsoft has released a new optional update for Windows 11. This update, known as KB5132057, is available for versions 25H2 and 26H2. It includes 28 changes and fixes to make the system run better.

One key change is to Windows Search. The search box now has a cleaner design and removes promotional content from web results. This makes the tool more efficient and easier to use. You can also complete tasks like turning on dark mode directly from the search bar.

The update also improves Windows Hello, the facial recognition feature. If you enable a specific setting, your computer can now recognise your face in dark rooms. This helps you sign in more easily when the lights are off.

Microsoft says this is the final non-security preview update for the year. Normal monthly updates will resume in January. The company also warned that some devices might restart one extra time during installation to update security certificates.

title: Ruby programming language fixes security flaw
text:
A fix is available for a weakness in Ruby that could allow attackers to disrupt services, though experts say it is hard to exploit.

The Ruby programming language has released updates to fix seven security weaknesses. The most serious issue, called Ruby2Shell, involves a mistake in how the software handles text. This error could potentially let an attacker run commands on a server.

According to SecurityWeek, the flaw occurs when changing the capitalisation of letters in certain text formats. For example, turning a specific German character into uppercase might cause the software to write data in the wrong place in memory. This could corrupt the system.

Experts from WatchTowr told SecurityWeek that successfully using this flaw to take over a system is very difficult. They said attackers would need very specific conditions to be met. It is more likely that bad requests would just stop the service from working, rather than giving hackers full control.

Patches for all seven issues are included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. The developers advise users to apply these fixes as soon as possible to stay safe.

title: F5 issues emergency fixes for critical security flaws
text:
A major US tech firm has released urgent updates to fix serious weaknesses in its network equipment, which could allow criminals to take control of systems.

US cybersecurity company F5 has warned customers to install emergency patches for five critical security flaws in its BIG-IP products. These weaknesses, known as remote code execution (RCE) flaws, allow attackers to run harmful commands on the device without needing a login. F5 said these issues are rated as critical severity.

The company also released a fix for a high-severity flaw that could cause the system to crash, a problem known as a denial-of-service (DoS) attack. F5 stated it has no other way to protect these systems besides installing the new updates. It advised security teams to apply the hotfixes released on Wednesday to vulnerable devices.

While F5 has not confirmed that these specific flaws are being used in attacks right now, it noted that cybercriminals and state-backed groups have often abused similar F5 vulnerabilities in the past. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has previously flagged other F5 flaws as actively exploited. Therefore, F5 recommends upgrading systems to the latest version as soon as possible.

title: Microsoft now auto-installs Windows 11 26H2 on home PCs
text:
Microsoft is automatically upgrading eligible personal computers to the latest Windows 11 version, so you may see the update without checking for it yourself.

Microsoft has started automatically installing Windows 11 26H2 on devices that are not managed by an IT department. This includes personal computers and business devices that do not have central IT control.

The update is rolling out to devices currently running Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2. Microsoft said this step makes it easier for users to get the latest version without manual intervention.

You can still choose to install the update yourself. To do this, go to Settings, then Windows Update, and select 'Check for Windows updates'. You can also turn on the option to get the latest updates as soon as they are available.

Microsoft confirmed that this month's security update for newer Windows 11 versions is causing some issues with installing or launching Office and other apps. The company is aware of these problems.

title: New tactic: delivery photo upload failure to steal your parcel
text:
Criminals are using a new trick to steal parcels by claiming a photo upload failed, leaving shoppers to fight for refunds.

Reports of parcel theft in the UK have nearly doubled in a year. A Freedom of Information request by parcel firm Quadient found 12,802 reports in the year to June, up from 6,851 the previous year. The true number is likely higher because not all police forces provided data and many crimes go unreported.

Which? has heard reports of a new tactic. A delivery driver takes a picture of your doorstep as proof of delivery. They then claim the image cannot be uploaded due to a technical problem. They take the parcel back, promising to redeliver it later. In reality, the parcel is marked as delivered, making it hard to get a refund.

There are also reports of drivers taking a photo of a front door and driving off without getting out of the van. One man, Jon Barnes, reportedly found his Amazon locker empty. He took a photo as evidence, but Amazon initially refused a refund and threatened to close his account. He later received a reimbursement after contacting Which? and police.

Consumer law says the retailer must prove safe delivery. However, in practice, you may need to provide evidence that a parcel was missing. Staffed collection points, like post offices, offer a human witness, which can help if a parcel goes missing.

title: Careers360 data breach
text:
Data allegedly taken from the Indian education and careers platform Careers360 appeared on a public hacking forum.

In November 2026, data allegedly taken from the Indian education and careers platform Careers360 appeared on a public hacking forum. The 22M records included 3.6M unique email addresses alongside names, phone numbers, genders and caste categories, and most also contained students' entrance exam results, including ranks and marks.

The breach was added to the Have I Been Pwned database on 20 November 2026. The source attributes the incident to a threat actor known as 'Threat Actor 888'.

title: Why storing work passwords in spreadsheets is risky
text:
Spreadsheets often miss new or changed passwords, leaving companies unaware of weak or shared logins that attackers can exploit.

The password spreadsheet your admins use may look like a complete inventory, but it only reflects some of the credentials employees have reported using. More specifically, that spreadsheet doesn’t show passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the document was last updated, until someone brings it up to date. That’s assuming someone ever does.

People often use easier methods to save passwords when official processes are slow. They might save logins in their web browser, send them in chat messages, or write them on sticky notes. A report by NordPass found that "123456" is the most common password used in a corporate setting. This shows that many people take the easy route when choosing passwords.

If a spreadsheet is out of date, it creates blind spots. Attackers who break into a company network often search for files with names like "password" or "login". If they find a spreadsheet, they can use the details inside to access other accounts. This can help them spread the attack further across the company.

To fix this, organisations need a better way to manage credentials. A business password manager provides a secure, central place to store work logins. It allows managers to see who has access to which accounts and check if passwords are weak or reused. This helps them spot problems early and keep company data safer.

title: Ofcom lists four ways to check if you are 16 for social media ban
text:
Ofcom has published a report identifying four reliable methods social media firms can use to verify users are over 16, ahead of the UK's upcoming ban.

Ofcom has published a rapid assessment on how social media companies can reliably determine if a user is aged 16 or over. This comes ahead of the UK Government setting out the practical rules for a social media ban for under-16s, which is expected to come into force next year.

The regulator identified four methods that are capable of being 'highly effective' at this age. These are photo ID matching, digital ID services, banking-based checks, and facial age estimation. Photo ID matching compares a document like a passport or driving licence to a live photo of the user. Banking checks use information held by a financial institution, while digital ID services allow people to prove their age online without repeatedly showing physical documents.

Facial age estimation uses technology to analyse a user's face to estimate their age. Because this method has a margin of error, Ofcom suggests it should be used alongside a second check, similar to how shops use 'Challenge 25' when selling alcohol. Ofcom notes that some 16 and 17-year-olds may need to obtain a photo ID to use these methods.

Ofcom says that while some children may still find ways to bypass these checks, the measures should significantly reduce the likelihood of under-16s accessing restricted sites. The regulator will monitor these attempts and publish research within twe

title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram feature launch
text:
The UK regulator is checking if Meta broke safety laws by launching a new Instagram feature without assessing risks to children.

Ofcom has opened a formal investigation into Meta. The regulator wants to know if the company failed to follow UK online safety laws.

In May, Meta launched a feature called Instants on Instagram. This allows users to share content that disappears after it has been viewed. Under the UK’s Online Safety Act, tech firms must check for risks before making big changes to their services.

Ofcom says providers must assess how their features might expose children to harmful material. They also must check for risks of illegal content. The regulator warned earlier this year that firms could face action if they skipped these checks.

George Lusty, Director of Enforcement at Ofcom, compared the process to testing a new car. He said safety must be built in from the start, not added later. If the investigation finds a breach, Ofcom can order fixes or impose fines of up to £18 million or 10% of global revenue.

title: PHP updates fix 18 security flaws, including critical bugs
text:
The PHP team has released updates to fix 18 security issues, some of which could let attackers control servers.

The team that develops PHP, a popular tool for building websites, has released new security updates. These updates fix 18 different flaws in the software.

Some of these flaws are described as critical. This means an attacker could potentially run code on a server without needing to log in first. This is known as remote code execution.

According to the report, the updates were released on Thursday, 19 November. They are available for all supported versions of PHP, including the latest releases.

The updates are designed to close these gaps before they can be used to harm websites or servers.

title: WhatsApp fixes flaw that may have been used to make scam messages look real
text:
WhatsApp has fixed a security gap that scammers may have used to make their messages appear more trustworthy on Android phones.

WhatsApp has patched a low-impact flaw in its Android apps. The company says it found the issue while disrupting a scam campaign. A WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek that they believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, is linked to 'Click to WhatsApp' ads. It affects both WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android. If a specific type of ad message was displayed, it could have revealed your IP address (your device's unique internet location) to an attacker.

WhatsApp also fixed two other medium-impact issues. One bug could have allowed an attacker to delete WhatsApp files if you tapped a malicious 'order details' message from an unofficial app. The other involved a security check for Meta AI. WhatsApp says there is no evidence that either of these was exploited.

The company has released updates to fix all three problems.

title: Bell Canada confirms data breach affecting business customers
text:
A Canadian telecoms firm says a hacker stole business contact details, but says no personal passwords or sensitive files were taken.

Bell Canada has confirmed that its systems were breached on 17 November 2026. The company says an "agentic" threat actor accessed its networks. This term suggests the attacker used AI-powered tools to carry out the attack.

According to Bell, the hacker stole data from a system used to order and set up telephone connections. The information may have been stolen includes business contact details, such as names, job titles, and work email addresses. It also includes some technical details about network connections.

Bell told BleepingComputer that the data did not contain passwords, highly sensitive personal information, or file attachments. The company said it quickly secured its systems and that customer services have not been affected.

Bell has not said how many businesses were affected or who is responsible for the attack. It is sharing security details with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security to help other organisations check for similar threats.

title: Singapore YMCA portal hit by data breach
text:
The YMCA of Singapore says its online application system was breached, exposing some personal details.

The YMCA of Singapore has confirmed a cybersecurity breach. It affected the online portal for its Youth For Causes programme. The organisation announced this on Saturday, 21 November 2026.

The breach involved the database linked to the application portal. This database held personal information about users. Some of this data included full or partial NRIC numbers.

The YMCA sent an email to participants and mentors on Saturday.

title: Microsoft fixes flaw that exposed business contact details
text:
Microsoft has fixed a security flaw in its Entra Connect Health service that allowed attackers to view some business contact details.

Microsoft says it found a weakness in its Entra Connect Health service on 9 November 2026. This service allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin centre. Attackers used this weakness to look at certain information about companies.

The company confirmed that attackers could see email addresses for technical contacts and administrators. They could also see basic details like company names and country codes. Microsoft says it did not find any evidence that attackers changed any settings or stole passwords.

Microsoft fixed the problem on 19 November 2026. It has now told affected businesses about the issue. The company has not said how many businesses were affected or who the attackers were.

Microsoft advises businesses to be careful. It warns that scammers might use the exposed email addresses to send fake messages. These messages, known as phishing, try to trick people into giving away more details.

title: Rackspace Spot breach exposed customer cloud secrets
text:
Hackers used stolen login details to access a cloud platform, potentially exposing sensitive passwords and keys for business customers.

Rackspace has warned that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform. The company said attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of the system on 17 November 2026. This allowed them to act like legitimate users in some customer organisations.

The attackers could create new workloads and read 'Kubernetes Secrets'. These are secure files that store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys. Rackspace warned that the hackers could have read any secret stored in an affected user's clusters.

Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on 18 November after a customer report. The company has since revoked affected tokens, removed unauthorised workloads, and rotated keys. It also strengthened access controls and monitoring to prevent further issues.

The breach caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console. This temporarily prevented customers from managing their clusters. Service was fully restored on 21 November 2026.

title: Michigan nurse jailed for Medicare fraud using stolen records
text:
A nurse in the US was sentenced to prison for billing Medicare for services that never happened, using stolen patient details.

Ruby Scott, a nurse from Farmington Hills, Michigan, has been sentenced to four years in federal prison. She owned a home health care company called Delta Home Health Care LLC. According to a press release from the Justice Department, she used stolen patient records to bill Medicare for fake services. The total value of the fraud scheme was reported as $1.6 million. Fox2 in Detroit reported that the sentencing took place on Thursday.

title: Criminals use phone calls to steal data from businesses
text:
A security firm says criminals are using phone calls to steal data.

Unit 42, a security team, has tracked several waves of attacks in recent months. These attacks are called vishing. This is a type of scam where criminals use phone calls to steal data.

The group behind these calls is linked to Com. Unit 42 says these attacks have led to data theft and attempts to demand money. The criminals targeted companies in industries that hold lots of personal data. This includes financial services, healthcare and legal services.

The main goal was to steal data and then use it for extortion.

This story is important because it shows how phone calls can be dangerous.

title: Cleverbridge breach exposes payment card details
text:
Cleverbridge says hackers stole payment card details, including security codes, from its online sales platform.

Cleverbridge is an online service that helps software companies sell products and process payments. The company says it detected unauthorised activity on 4 November 2026. It temporarily took its systems offline to contain the breach.

Cleverbridge confirmed that a third party copied payment card data. A notification sent to customers reveals that the stolen information includes card numbers, expiry dates, and CVV codes.

The company says it did not steal other personal data, such as names or billing addresses. It has not said how many customers were affected or how the attackers got in. Cleverbridge has told data protection authorities and law enforcement about the incident.

The company is working with TransUnion to send out notifications. It is also offering free credit monitoring to affected customers to help them track their accounts.

title: Phone company fined £437,500 for letting scammers use its numbers
text:
Ofcom has fined Tismi for failing to stop scammers from using phone numbers it provided, putting consumers at risk of fraud.

Ofcom has fined telecoms provider Tismi £437,500. The regulator found that Tismi failed to take proper steps to prevent its phone numbers from being misused by scammers. This failure lasted from November 2022 to January 2025. During this time, approximately 366,000 numbers were exposed to potential misuse.

Phone companies must check their business customers to stop scammers getting valid numbers. They must also monitor for misuse and handle reports properly. Ofcom found that Tismi did not carry out these checks or have the right systems in place. It also lacked a formal process for dealing with reports of misuse.

Ofcom Director of Enforcement George Lusty said there is no excuse for failing to put proper checks in place. He stated that companies putting customers at the mercy of scammers will face consequences. The fine will be passed to HM Treasury. Tismi received a 30% discount on the fine because it admitted liability.

As part of the decision, Tismi must now prove it is following the rules. It must provide details of its new checks and monitoring processes. Ofcom has also opened a new investigation into another company, Xtra Phones UK, over similar concerns about number misuse.

title: Ofcom warns about 'job offer' and missed call phone scams
text:
Criminals are using automated voices and quick hang-ups to trick you into calling back, so you should hang up and report these calls.

Ofcom has warned the public about two common types of scam phone calls. One uses an automated voice to claim you have a job offer. The other is a call from an unknown number that hangs up after just a few moments.

These calls are designed to make you call the number back. Once you are on the line, criminals try to pressure you into giving away sensitive personal details or making payments to accounts they control. You could also accidentally call a premium-rate number and run up a large bill.

Ofcom says the number of people reporting suspicious calls has fallen over the last four years. However, the regulator is still investigating four telecoms providers as part of its ongoing work to tackle phone scams.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Tackling this complex problem requires a joined-up approach from Government, other regulators, law enforcement and industry.” They noted that telecoms companies are already blocking millions of scam calls every month.
